was standing when you first saw him?"

"Just by the dressing-table, here, under the light."

"And where did you say that you were standing?"

"I was at the door here, when I first saw him."

"And the door was open?"

"Yes; I have told you so."

"So you saw him from the doorway, with the coronet in his hand,
standing by the dressing-table?"

"Precisely."

"And the window?"

"The window was closed and fastened."

"I should like to have a word with the house-maid, Lucy Parr."

"She is in the kitchen," said Mr. Holder.

"Wait, I will fetch her for you."

But before he could move, the girl herself entered the room. She
was a very pretty girl, with a bright, intelligent face and a
neat, trim figure.

"You wished to speak to me, sir?" she said, addressing Holmes.

"Yes. You were out last night, were you not?"

"I was, sir. I went to the gate to see a friend."

"A friend? Who was this friend?"

"It was only a young man, sir."

"His name?"

"Francis Prosper, sir."

"And what is he?"

"He is a greengrocer's assistant, sir."

"I see. And you were at the side gate?"

"Yes, sir."

"For how long?"

"Oh, for only a few minutes, sir."

"And you saw no one else?"

"No one, sir."

"Thank you; that will do."

The girl curtsied and left the room.

"Now," said Holmes, "I should like to see the page."

The page was a small, sharp-looking boy of twelve or thirteen. He
could tell us nothing, however, except that he had been asleep
all night and had heard nothing.

"And now, Mr. Holder," said Holmes, "I think that I have seen all
that I wish to see here. I shall return to London now, but I hope
to be able to give you some more definite news by to-morrow
morning."

"You have no doubt as to Arthur's guilt?"

"I have already told you that I cannot speak as confidently as
you do. There are several points which are still to be
explained."

"But the gems! What has become of the gems?"

"I hope to be able to tell you that also by to-morrow morning."

"I shall be most anxious to hear from you. Good-bye, Mr. Holmes."

"Good-bye."

We walked back to the station together, and as we went Holmes
seemed to be more than usually thoughtful. He hardly spoke a word
the whole way to London, and it was not until we were back in our
rooms in Baker Street that he broke his silence.

"A very pretty little problem, Watson," said he, as he threw
himself into his armchair and lit his pipe. "A very pretty little
problem indeed."

"You have some theory, then?"

"I have several. But they are all more or less vague at present.
The case is a very remarkable one. What did you think of the
niece, Mary?"

"She seemed to be a very charming and sensible young lady."

"And her paleness? Did you notice her paleness?"

"Yes; she looked very ill."

"She did indeed. And her uncle's description of her? A sunbeam in
the house, a wonderful manager and housekeeper, and yet as tender
and quiet and gentle as a woman could be. A very charming picture,
Watson."

"And the son, Arthur? What did you think of him?"

"I have not seen him yet. But his father's description of him is
hardly so charming. A disappointment, wild, wayward, a member of
an aristocratic club, a player of cards and a squanderer of
money. Not a very promising character, Watson."

"And the friend, Sir George Burnwell?"

"A man of the world to his finger-tips, a brilliant talker, and a
man of great personal beauty. Yet a man who should be deeply
distrusted. A very interesting character, Watson."

"And the house-maid, Lucy Parr?"

"A very pretty girl, and one who has attracted admirers. A
greengrocer's assistant, for example."

"And the page?"

"A small, sharp-looking boy. But he knew nothing."

"And the coronet?"

"Ah, the coronet! A very precious public possession. Thirty-nine
enormous beryls, and the price of the gold chasing incalculable.
A very valuable piece of jewellery, Watson."

"And the missing piece?"

"Three beryls. And the gold corner. A very significant fact,
Watson."

"How so?"

"Because it would take a very strong man to break off a piece of
solid gold like that. Arthur is strong, his father says. But
would even he be strong enough to do it with his hands alone?"

"You think, then, that he must have used some instrument?"

"It is possible. But if so, where is the instrument? No such
instrument was found in his room or on his person."

"Perhaps he threw it out of the window?"

"The window was closed and fastened."

"Then what is your theory?"

"I have several, as I told you. But they are all more or less
vague at present. I must think it over, Watson. I must think it
over."

He sat for some time in silence, puffing at his pipe and staring
into the fire. Then he rose and went to his desk, where he spent
the rest of the evening in making notes and calculations. I left
him there when I went to bed, and when I came down to breakfast
the next morning I found him still at work.

"You have been up all night?" I asked.

"No; I have had a few hours' sleep. But I have been busy since
four o'clock."

"And have you come to any conclusion?"

"I think so. I think that I can see light at last."

"And the gems? Have you found them?"

"I hope to have them in my hands before the day is out."

"And the thief? Have you discovered him?"

"I think so. I think that I can name the man."

"Who is he, then?"

"I shall not tell you yet, Watson. I must be sure of my facts
before I speak. But I have a little business to attend to this
morning, and if you have nothing better to do, perhaps you would
like to come with me."

"I should be delighted."

"Then we will set off at once. We have no time to lose."

"I see no reason to believe anything else," said Sherlock Holmes,
appearing at the door, "although I have not yet found the
evidence to prove it. Is this Miss Mary, the young lady of whom I
have heard?"

"Yes, she is my niece."

"I have been making a few observations outside," said Holmes,
"and I have come to the conclusion that I must see the
house-maid, Lucy Parr. She came in by the back door late
yesterday evening, did she not?"

"I saw her myself," said Mary.

"She is a very pretty girl, is she not?"

"Yes, but she is quite a well-behaved girl. She is not a person
of whom I have ever had any reason to complain."

"Could I see her?"

"Certainly."

"One moment," said Holmes, as the banker was about to ring the
bell. "I should like to look at the room where the robbery was
committed."

"This way, then."

We followed our host into the drawing-room and from there to his
own dressing-room. The bureau stood in the corner, and the
jewel-case was upon it. Holmes examined them both with his
customary minuteness.

"You have no idea, I suppose, where the three beryls have
gone?"

"None."

"And your son, also, can give no information?"

"No, he will not speak a word."

"That is very strange. And what was he doing when you first saw
him? Was he kneeling, or standing?"

"He was standing, and appeared to be bending the coronet in his
hands."

"Exactly. And you see that it is bent?"

"It is, very slightly."

"And do you think that a man could bend that gold with his
hands? It is a solid band of gold, nearly half an inch thick."

"I should have thought it impossible."

"And yet you thought that your son had not only bent it but
broken a piece off it with his hands. Just try for yourself."

The banker took the coronet and strained at it. "No," said he, "I
cannot even move it."

"Then what makes you think that your son could? It would take a
very strong man to do it, and even then he would require some
sort of leverage. No, the thing is impossible. And now, if you
please, I should like to see Lucy Parr."

"It is not only his innocence, Miss Mary," said Holmes, "which
interests me, but also the recovery of the gems. We cannot,
however, hope for much for some time. I have been all round the
house, and I am fairly satisfied that no one has left it from
the inside during the night. But what of the windows?"

"The windows have all been examined by the police, and they are
not only fastened but their fastenings are so old and rusty that
it would be almost impossible for any one to have tampered with
them from the outside. The only window which can be opened from
the outside is the hall window, and that was closed and bolted
by me just before I went to bed."

"Did you see anyone outside at the time?"

"No, I saw no one."

"And you have no doubt that no one could have entered the house
from the outside during the night?"

"None whatever."

"And you, Mr. Holder?"

"I am as certain as I can be of anything that the house was
perfectly secure until I myself came downstairs and opened the
front door this morning."

"The front door is not a very safe place, I should think," said
Holmes. "I see that you have a double lock, and that it is
further secured by a heavy bar. Now, how about the back door? It
is usually left only on the latch, I suppose?"

"No, I myself see to its being locked every night."

"You are very careful, I see. Now, how about the side window?
Was that also locked?"

"I did it myself."

"And the window at which you were standing, Miss Mary? You say
that you closed it and fastened it yourself?"

"Yes."

"And you saw no one?"

"No one."

"Wait a moment! Did you not say, Mr. Holder, that your niece
informed you that she had seen the maid, Lucy Parr, coming in by
the back door?"

"Yes, I did."

"And what did Lucy Parr say for herself?"

"She said that she had only been to the gate to speak to a
friend."

"A friend? A man?"

"Yes, she has a sweetheart, a greengrocer's man who lives in the
neighbourhood. I believe his name is Francis Prosper."

"I see. Now, let us go and have a look at the room where the
coronet was kept."

"I share your hope, Miss Holder," said Holmes, who had entered the room so silently that we were none of us aware of his presence until he spoke. He stood with his back to the fire, his hands in his pockets, and a look of intense concentration upon his face. "The snow is a grand tell-tale, Mr. Holder, and it has already whispered some very singular things into my ear. If you will be so good as to allow me, I should like to examine the premises a little more closely, but first, there is a small matter of detail. I should like to see the girl, Lucy Parr, and to hear from her own lips her account of her movements last night."

"I fully share your opinion, and I trust, with you, that we may
prove it," returned Holmes, going back to the mat to knock the
snow from his shoes. "I believe I have the honour of addressing
Miss Mary Holder. Might I ask you a question or two?"

"Pray do, sir, if it may help to clear this horrible affair up."

"You heard nothing yourself last night?"

"Nothing, until my uncle here began to speak loudly. I heard
that, and I came down."

"You shut up the windows and doors the night before. Did you
fasten all the windows?"

"Yes."

"Were they all fastened this morning?"

"Yes."

"You have a maid who has a sweetheart? I think that you remarked
to your uncle last night that she had been out to see him?"

"Yes, and she was the girl who waited in the drawing-room, and
who may have heard uncle's remarks about the coronet."

"I see. You infer that she may have gone out to tell her
sweetheart, and that the two may have planned the robbery."

"But what is the good of all these vague theories," cried the
banker impatiently, "when I have told you that I saw Arthur with
the coronet in his hands?"

"Wait a little, Mr. Holder. We must come back to that. About this
girl, Miss Holder. You saw her return by the kitchen door, I
presume?"

"Yes; when I went to see if the door was fastened for the night I
met her slipping in. I saw the man, too, in the gloom."

"Do you know him?"

"Oh, yes! he is the green-grocer who brings our vegetables round.
His name is Francis Prosper."

"He stood," said Holmes, "to the left of the door--that is to
say, farther up the path than is necessary to reach the door?"

"Yes, he did."

"And he is a man with a wooden leg?"

He walked rapidly from one to the other of the windows upon the ground floor, pausing only at the large one which looked out upon the stable lane. He opened this and examined the sill very carefully with a convex lens. "I see nothing here," said he at last. "Let us go upstairs and look at the bureau." We followed him to the dressing-room, where he spent some time in a minute examination of the furniture. The bureau was a plain, old-fashioned piece of walnut-wood, with a sloping top and a small shelf above it. Holmes scrutinized the lock and the wood-work around it, but there were no signs of violence. Then, taking the key from the banker, he opened it and looked inside.

He passed rapidly from one to the other until he came to the large window which looked out upon the stable lane. This he opened and examined the sill with his pocket lens. "Now," said he at last, "let us go up to the dressing-room." We followed him up the broad, oak-panelled staircase to the room where the events of the night had occurred. It was a plainly furnished little chamber, with a grey carpet, a large bureau, and a long mirror. Holmes went to the bureau first and looked hard at the lock.

He passed rapidly from window to window around the house, but it was not until he reached the side which faced the lane that he showed any signs of interest. This was the window in the hall which Miss Holder had been seen to close on the previous night. Holmes stood before it for some minutes, looking now at the sill, now at the ground, and now at the wooden fence which separated the garden from the lane. Then he opened the window and, stepping out, he spent some time in the snow upon the other side. Finally he returned, his face set and grim, and we followed him as he made his way upstairs to the dressing-room where the robbery had been committed.

He walked swiftly round from one to the other, pausing only at the large window which looked out upon the stable lane, and which Miss Holder had mentioned that she had fastened the night before. Thence he passed into the hall, and we all followed him up the stairs to the dressing-room. It was a small, comfortably furnished room, with a grey carpet and a large bureau of dark wood standing in the corner between the two windows. Holmes went straight to the bureau and examined the lock with the greatest care.

He passed rapidly from window to window upon the ground floor,
pausing for some time at the large one which looked out upon the
stable lane. He then walked into the hall and opened the window
at which Miss Holder had been seen the night before, leaning out
to examine the sill with his pocket lens. "This is very
suggestive," he remarked as he closed it again. "Now, Mr. Holder,
if you will be so good as to lead the way, we will examine the
upper floor and the scene of the struggle."

He walked swiftly round from one to the other, pausing only at
the large one which looked from the hall onto the stable lane.
This he opened and made a very careful examination of the sill
with his powerful magnifying lens. "Now we shall go upstairs,"
said he at last.

The banker's dressing-room was a plainly furnished little
chamber, with a grey carpet, a large bureau, and a long mirror.
Holmes went to the bureau first and looked hard at the lock.

"Which key was used to open it?" he asked.

"That which my son himself indicated--that of the cupboard of the
lumber-room."

"Have you it here?"

"That is it on the dressing-table."

Sherlock Holmes took it up and opened the bureau.

"And I should be happy to show you how easy it is to do,"
responded Holmes, and as he spoke he began to bend the coronet
with all his might. "You have no idea what a difficult thing it
is to break," he continued. "There! I have it now." As he spoke,
there was a snap, and the gold-work gave way.

The banker sat down on his chair and gazed at Holmes with such
a look of horror that I could see that he began to think my
friend as mad as himself.

"But it will not go back!" he gasped. "It is ruined!"

"I am showing you that it is no easy thing for a man, however
powerful, to break off a corner such as this. You must admit
that."

"It has gone beyond my strength, I think," said the banker.

"Precisely. And do you think that it could be done without a
loud snap being heard all over the house? That noise was what
woke you up, Mr. Holder."

"And Arthur was there when it was done?"

"But he was not the only one there. We must think who could have
broken it. If your son had broken it, he would have done it in
the next room, not in your dressing-room. And he would have done
it where he could not have been heard. We must look further
into the matter."

"How? Where?"

"We must go outside once more, and look for further clues."

"But what clues can there be in the snow? It is all trampled
down and frozen."

"That is exactly what I like to see," said Holmes, and we
followed him once more out into the cold morning air.

"You will then allow me to try." Sherlock Holmes took the gold
piece between his powerful fingers and wrenched at it until his
face grew crimson and his veins stood out on his forehead. "I
will not try any further," said he, letting go of the coronet and
wiping his brow. "I could not even move it, and it would need a
man with a very powerful pair of hands to break it. You heard a
snap, did you not, Mr. Holder?"

"Yes, like a pistol-shot."

"That is exactly what I should have expected. Yet your son told
you that he had heard no snap?"

"None."

"Then there is another point which tells in his favour. It is
extremely unlikely that he could have broken that off without
making a loud noise. I am quite certain now that he is innocent.
I have seen all that I wish to see in this house, and I think
that we should return to Baker Street."

"What! Without finding the gems?"

"I think that I can find them for you. Now, if you please, we
shall go back to the City together."

"Then you think that the jewels were not in the house?"

"Certainly not."

"And Arthur?"

"He is in prison, but he will be released to-morrow. In the
meantime, I will go back and prepare for what is to follow. If
you will call upon me at eleven o'clock to-morrow morning I
think that I shall be able to place the missing stones in your
hands."

The banker's face was a study of joy and astonishment.

"God bless you, Mr. Holmes!" he cried. "But you do not mean that
you really know who has taken them?"

"I am quite certain of it."

"And where they are?"

"I think that I shall be able to tell you that to-morrow."

"Is it Arthur, then?"

"I have already told you that he is innocent."

"Then who is it? Is it Sir George Burnwell?"

"I have my suspicions, but I would rather not say anything
definite at present. We must have patience for a few hours. I
shall see you at eleven o'clock to-morrow morning."

"Then I will," said Holmes, and to my amazement he threw his whole
strength upon it and wrenched at it with such force that it shook
the room. "You see," said he at last, "it is not so easy to break
this gold as it is to break a twig. It took all my strength to
try and move it, and yet I have not succeeded in the least. And
now, I ask you, could your son have done it? He could not. If he
had, he must have been a Hercules. This gold is not meant to be
broken in that way. It is meant to be handled with care. If a man
wished to break off a portion of it he would have to use some
instrument, and that would leave its mark on the gold. No,
Arthur Holder is as innocent as you or I."

"Then where are the stones?" cried the banker.

"That is what we have to find out. I must go over the house
again, and then I must go out into the garden and the lane. I
think I have a pretty clear idea of the whole affair now."

He spent a long time in the garden, and he walked several times
to and fro in the lane, until at last he returned to the house,
shivering with cold and his face radiant with satisfaction.

"I have done all that I can for you to-day, Mr. Holder," said he.
"I shall return to London, but I shall be back here to-morrow.
I have much to think about and to do, and I will let you know
the result of my inquiries by then."

"But what of Arthur? What of my son? What of the jewels?"

"Have patience, my dear sir. I have strong hopes that all will be
right."

He took his hat and we went off together, leaving the banker in a
state of the greatest excitement and suspense. When we reached
the station, Holmes turned to me with a smile.

"What do you think of it, Watson?" he asked.

"I am quite at a loss," I answered. "The whole thing is a
mystery to me."

"It is certainly a very interesting case," said he. "There are
some points in it which I should like to be more clear about, but
I think that I see my way through it now. We must have a look at
Sir George Burnwell."

"Sir George Burnwell! Why, what has he to do with it?"

"A great deal, I think. He is an old friend of Arthur's, you
know, and has a great influence over him. He is a man of the
world, and a gambler, and altogether a very dangerous companion
for a young man like Arthur. I think that we shall find that he
has had something to do with this business."

"But how?"

"That is what we have to find out. But I have a theory which I
think will work. We shall see."

We reached Baker Street in time for dinner, and Holmes spent the
evening in his armchair, with his eyes closed and his pipe in his
mouth, as was his custom when he was thinking deeply. I knew
that he was working out the details of the case, and I did not
disturb him.

The next morning he was up early, and after breakfast he asked
me to accompany him to Streatham. When we reached the house we
found Mr. Holder in a state of great anxiety.

"Have you found anything?" he asked, as soon as we entered the
room.

"I have found a good deal," said Holmes. "But I have not yet
found the jewels. I hope to do so, however, before long."

"But where are they?"

"That is what I am going to find out. I must have another look at
the garden and the lane."

He spent some time in the garden, and then he went out into the
lane. I followed him, and I saw him looking very closely at the
snow. Suddenly he stopped and pointed to a spot where the snow
had been trampled.

"Look here, Watson," he said. "Do you see these footprints?"

"Yes," I answered. "They are very distinct."

"They are the footprints of a man with a wooden leg," said
Holmes. "And they lead straight to the window of the hall."

"Francis Prosper!" I cried.

"Precisely. And here are some other footprints, which lead away
from the window. They are the footprints of a man in his
stocking-feet."

"Arthur Holder!"

"Exactly. Now, let us follow these footprints and see where they
lead."

We followed the footprints of the man with the wooden leg, and
they led us to a small wooden shed at the end of the garden.
Holmes opened the door and we went in. The shed was empty, save
for a few garden tools and some old boxes.

"Nothing here," said Holmes. "Let us look at the other
footprints."

We followed the footprints of the man in his stocking-feet, and
they led us to the stable lane. There they were lost in the
trampled snow of the road.

"This is very strange," said Holmes. "Wait a moment. What is
this?"

He stooped down and picked up something from the snow. It was a
small piece of gold, with a beryl in it.

"The missing jewels!" I cried.

"One of them," said Holmes. "But where are the others? And who
is the thief?"

"It must be Arthur," I said. "He was seen with the coronet in his
hands, and his footprints lead to the spot where this was found."

"But why should he steal it?" asked Holmes. "He could have had it
whenever he wanted it. And why should he break it? It would be
much easier to take the whole thing."

"Perhaps he wanted to sell the stones separately," I suggested.

"But why should he return with the rest of the coronet? No,
Watson, there is something more in this than meets the eye. Let
us go back to the house and see what we can find there."

When we reached the house we found Mr. Holder and Mary in the
dining-room.

"Have you found anything?" asked the banker.

"I have found one of the beryls," said Holmes, showing it to him.

"Thank God!" cried the banker. "But where are the others?"

"That is what I am going to find out," said Holmes. "But first I
must ask Miss Holder a few questions."

He turned to Mary, who was looking very pale and agitated.

"Miss Holder," he said, "I believe that you are in the habit of
sitting in the hall window in the evening?"

"Yes," she answered. "I like to look out at the garden."

"And you were sitting there on the night of the robbery?"

"Yes."

"Did you see anyone in the garden?"

"No one."

"Are you quite sure?"

"Quite sure."

"And yet we have found the footprints of a man with a wooden leg
leading straight to that window."

Mary turned even paler than before.

"I--I may have been mistaken," she stammered. "I--I think I did
see someone."

"And who was it?"

"It was--it was Francis Prosper."

"And what was he doing?"

"He was--he was looking in at the window."

"And did you speak to him?"

"No, I was frightened and I ran away."

"I see. And now, Miss Holder, I must ask you one more question.
Do you know Sir George Burnwell?"

"Yes," she answered. "He is a friend of Arthur's."

"Is he a friend of yours, too?"

"No," she said, with a look of distaste. "I do not like him."

"I see. Well, I think that is all for the present. I shall return
to London now, and I shall be back here to-morrow."

"But what about Arthur?" asked the banker. "Will you not do
something for him?"

"I am doing everything I can," said Holmes. "And I have strong
hopes that I shall be able to prove his innocence before long."

He took his hat and we went off together. When we reached the
station, Holmes turned to me with a look of triumph.

"I think I have it now, Watson," he said. "I think I have it
now."

"What is it?" I asked.

"It is a very clever plot," he said. "A very clever plot indeed.
But I think I have seen through it. We shall see to-morrow."

The next morning we returned to Streatham. When we reached the
house we found Mr. Holder and Mary in the dining-room. Holmes
went straight to the banker and handed him a small package.

"Here are the other two beryls, Mr. Holder," he said.

"Thank God!" cried the banker. "But where did you find them?"

"I found them in the possession of the real thief," said Holmes.

"And who is the thief?"

"The thief is Sir George Burnwell," said Holmes.

"Sir George Burnwell!" cried the banker. "But how? Why?"

"It is a long story," said Holmes. "But I will tell it to you
now. Sir George Burnwell is a man of the world, a gambler, and a
villain. He has been using his influence over Arthur to get money
from him, and when Arthur could not give him any more he decided
to steal the Beryl Coronet. He knew that Arthur would be the one
suspected, and he hoped that he would be able to get away with
the jewels while Arthur was in prison. He had an accomplice in
the house--Lucy Parr, the maid--who told him about the coronet and
where it was kept. On the night of the robbery he came to the
house and met Lucy at the side gate. She gave him the key to the
bureau, and he went into the house and took the coronet. He
tried to break off a piece of it, but he could not, so he used a
pair of pliers to wrench off the corner with the three beryls. He
then gave the rest of the coronet back to Lucy, who put it back
in the bureau. But Arthur had seen him through the window, and he
rushed out and tried to stop him. They had a struggle in the
lane, and Arthur managed to get the corner with the three beryls
away from him. But in the struggle he dropped one of the beryls
in the snow, and the other two remained in his hand. He was
returning to the house to put them back when he was discovered by
his father. He did not want to betray Sir George, because he was
his friend, and he did not want to betray Lucy, because he knew
that she was in love with Sir George and had been led astray by
him. So he remained silent, even when he was accused of the
theft. But I have found the other two beryls in Sir George's
rooms in London, and I have also found a pair of pliers with
traces of gold on them. So the case is clear."

"And what of Lucy Parr?" asked the banker.

"She has confessed everything," said Holmes. "She was lead astray
by Sir George, who promised to marry her if she would help him.
She is very sorry for what she has done, and I think that she
should be forgiven."

"And Arthur?"

"Arthur is a hero," said Holmes. "He has suffered in silence to
protect his friend and the woman his friend loved. He should be
honoured, not punished."

The banker was overcome with emotion. He took Arthur's hand and
implored his forgiveness. And Arthur, with a smile, forgave him.

"And now, Watson," said Holmes, as we were returning to London,
"I think we have done a good day's work. The Beryl Coronet is
safe, and the real thief is in the hands of the police. It is a
very satisfactory conclusion to a very interesting case."

"It is indeed," I said. "And I am glad that Arthur is cleared."

"So am I," said Holmes. "He is a brave young man, and I am sure
that he will make a great success of his life now that he is free
from the influence of Sir George Burnwell."

And so the mystery of the Beryl Coronet was solved, and Sherlock
Holmes once more proved himself to be the greatest detective of
his age.

"You must," said Holmes. "I should not wish to do it myself, and
I do not care to ask my friend, Watson, but I must know if you,
a strong man, can by any possibility wrench a corner of this off
with your own hands."

Mr. Holder took it up with a shudder and put forth his whole
strength, but it did not move. He was quite unable to make the
slightest impression upon the gold.

"You see," said Holmes, "that you cannot do it. Is it not so?"

"I cannot."

"Then do you think it is likely that your son, who is but a young
man and not by any means a giant, could have done so?"

"I think not. I should not like to say that he could."

"Wait a moment. We will see if it could be done by any other
means. Now, Watson, if you would be so kind as to give me the
heavy poker from the fire-place."

I handed him the poker, and with a sudden blow he struck the
remaining corner of the coronet. It bent, but it did not break.
Then, taking it in his hands, he twisted it until with a sharp
crack it snapped in two.

"You see," said he, "it took a heavy blow and a great deal of
force to break it. And it did not break noiselessly. Did you hear
no such sound as that last night?"

"None."

"Then I think that we may safely conclude that it was not broken
in your room. And now, Mr. Holder, if you will allow me to take
these two pieces of the coronet with me, and if you will permit
me to look over your garden once more, I think that I shall have
seen enough to form a very clear idea of the case."

"Precisely. It would take a great deal of force to do so. It is a
singularly strong diadem. I have been considered a man of no
mean strength, and yet I do not think that I could break this off
with my hands alone. And the gold work, look at it; do you see
any trace of a break? No; it is only twisted. It would take a
very strong pair of pliers to take that piece off. Now, I shall
ask you once more, what was it that Arthur was doing when you
saw him?"

"He was trying to wrench at the coronet," said the banker, with a
shudder.

"Precisely. He was trying to straighten it. He had found it
twisted, and was trying to put it right. He would not tell you
so, for his pride was hurt by your suspicions. That is my view
of the case, and I have found nothing to contradict it. But we
have still to find where the three missing stones are, and what
was his reason for being so silent as to how he became possessed
of the coronet."

"But if he were innocent, who could have done it?"

"We must find that out," returned Holmes. "I should like now to
go out for a few minutes and make some further investigations
among the servants."

"Shall I call them up for you?"

"No, I would rather speak to them alone, if you do not mind."

He left the room, and we were left together in the banker's
dressing-room. My friend was not away for more than ten minutes.
When he returned his face was still as impassive as ever, and I
could learn nothing from it.

"Now, Mr. Holder," said he, "I think that I have learned all that
it is possible to learn here. We will return to Baker Street by
the next train."

"But the stones, Mr. Holmes! The stones!"

"I have no doubt that they will be recovered. I should be glad,
however, if you would give me a little more information about
the girl Lucy Parr."

"She is a very good girl," said the banker, "and I have no
suspicion of her. I have known her for years."

"She has a sweetheart, you say?"

"Yes, a green-grocer with a wooden leg."

"I see. Now, Mr. Holder, if you will follow my advice, you will
remain at home for the next few days. I shall probably have
something to tell you by that time."

"But the police! What am I to tell them?"

"Tell them nothing. I will take all responsibility. Good-day to
you."

On our way back to Baker Street, Holmes was as silent as before,
and it was only when we were back in our room that he began to
speak.

"The case is a very pretty one, Watson," said he, "but it is not
so simple as I at first thought. We have to deal with some very
clever people."

"But who can have committed the robbery?" I asked.

"Well, it is not yet clear, but I have some ideas. I have been
making a few inquiries about Sir George Burnwell."

"And what have you found out?"

"That he is a man of very doubtful character. He has been in
many a shady transaction, and I should not be surprised if he
were at the bottom of this business. But we must have more
evidence before we can be sure."

"Then I will." Holmes suddenly bent his strength upon it, but
without result. "I feel it give a little," said he; "but, though
I am exceptionally strong in the fingers, it would take me all my
time to break it. An ordinary man could not do it. Now, what do
you think would happen if I did break it, Mr. Holder? There would
be a noise like a pistol shot. Do you tell me that all this
happened within a few yards of your bed and that you heard
nothing of it?"

"I do not know what to think. It is all dark to me."

"But perhaps it may grow lighter as we go. What do you think,
Miss Holder?"

"I confess that I still share my uncle's perplexity."

"Your son had no shoes or slippers on when you saw him?"

"He had nothing on save only his trousers and shirt."

He went out alone, for he had a way of close observation which could not be performed while he was being watched. From the window I could see him pacing up and down the stable lane, his head sunk upon his chest, and his hands behind his back. Once or twice he knelt down in the snow, and once he appeared to be measuring something with a tape. He was away for nearly an hour before he returned, with his boots white with snow and his face more inscrutable than ever.

He went out alone, for he explained that any fresh footprints might confuse his observations. For nearly an hour he remained away, while we waited in the dining-room, Mary Holder sitting with her head in her hands, and the banker pacing the room with nervous, jerky steps. At last, however, our messenger of hope returned. He had removed his boots, and his stockings were soaked with the melting snow, but he looked like a man who was well satisfied with his morning's work.

He went out alone, but I could see him through the hall window as he wandered about in the snow. He spent a considerable time in the stable lane, where the ground was relatively undisturbed, and I watched him as he moved slowly along, his head bent, his eyes fixed upon the white surface. Twice he knelt down, and once he appeared to be measuring something with his pocket-tape. He then moved to the small thicket by the tradesmen's entrance, and finally back to the front of the house. When he re-entered the room, his face was alert and his eyes had the bright, hard look which they wore when he was on a hot scent.

He went alone, however, for he could easily see that I was tired and that Mr. Holder was in no state to accompany him. I watched him from the window as he paced up and down the garden, and finally vanished round the corner of the house. It was nearly an hour before he returned, but I could see by his face that he had not been idle. His boots were covered with snow, and his expression was that of a man who has at last seen his way through a difficult problem.

He went out alone, and we saw him from the window as he paced slowly up and down the garden, his head sunk upon his chest and his hands behind his back. He stopped once or twice and examined the snow, particularly where it had been disturbed near the stable lane, and once he climbed upon the wall and looked over into the thoroughfare beyond. Then he returned to the house, his face more animated than I had seen it since he had started upon the case. "I think that I have seen all that there is to see," he remarked as he re-entered the hall, shaking the snow from his sleeves. "It is a most suggestive little problem, and I am glad that I came down to look into it. Miss Holder, I should be much obliged to you if you would tell me where Lucy Parr, the maid, is at present?"

He went alone, at his own request, for he explained that any
unnecessary footmarks might make his task more difficult. For an
hour or more he was at work, returning at last with his feet
heavy with snow and his features as inscrutable as ever.

"I think that I have seen now all that there is to see, Mr.
Holder," said he; "I can serve you best by returning to my
rooms."

"But the gems, Mr. Holmes. Where are they?"

"I cannot tell."

The banker wrung his hands. "I shall never see them again!" he
cried. "And my son? You give me hopes?"

"My opinion is in no way altered."

"Then, for God's sake, what was this dark business which was
acted in my house last night?"

It was clear to me that my companion had some very definite clue
in his mind, though he was not yet ready to share it with me. On
the way back to the city he stopped at a telegraph office and
sent off several messages. After our arrival at Baker Street he
did not sit down, but hurried into his bedroom and emerged ten
minutes later in the character of a common loafer. With his
collar turned up, a red neckerchief, and a worn-out coat, he was
so completely transformed that I could hardly believe my eyes.
He nodded to me with a grin and slipped out into the snowy
street, leaving me to spend the remainder of the afternoon in a
fever of curiosity as to what strange quest my friend had
embarked upon.

It was easy to see that my friend had conceived some system which answered to all the facts of the case, though I confess that I was as much in the dark as ever. Several times during our homeward journey I endeavoured to sound him upon the point, but he always gave a tactical turn to the conversation, until at last I gave it up in despair. It was not until we had reached our rooms and he had exchanged his boots for slippers that he even began to speak of the matter, and even then it was only to ask for the loan of my thickest overcoat and a heavy silk muffler.

It was evident to me that my companion had some very definite
clue in his mind, though I could not for the life of me imagine
whence it could have come or whither it led. During our
journey back to the City he was submerged in one of those
profound silences which always preceded his most brilliant
coups. I, for my part, was busy pondering the various facts of
the case—the wooden-legged man, the maid, the silent son, and
the pale, anxious niece—but I could find no thread to connect
them. It was late in the afternoon before we reached Baker
Street, and Holmes, instead of taking his usual seat by the
fire, began to busy himself with his chemicals, only to dash
out again at dusk, having first changed his attire for a
costume which would have made him at home in the roughest
quarters of the town.

It was clear to me that my companion had already conceived some system of his own, for his manner was more alert and his eyes had lost the look of abstraction which had clouded them during our journey to Streatham. We reached the station in silence, and it was not until we were once more ensconced in our Baker Street rooms that he spoke of the matter. "I have the threads in my hands, Watson," he remarked, as he threw off his overcoat and reached for his pipe. "The case is almost complete, though there are still some gaps to be filled before I can present the whole truth to our client. I shall be out for some hours now, and I must ask you to excuse me. It is a matter which requires delicate handling, and I must play my own hand."

It was evident to me that my companion had already formed some very definite theory in his mind, for his eyes sparkled and his manner was more alert than it had been since the start of the case. He did not speak a word during our journey back to London, but he paced the platform while we waited for our train with a feverish energy which told of the activity of his brain. No sooner had we reached our rooms in Baker Street than he began to show that he was on the scent of some fresh discovery. He threw off his heavy overcoat and, having snatched a piece of bread from the table, he began to busy himself with a pair of old shoes and a bundle of rags which he drew from the bottom of his cupboard.

It was obvious to me that my companion's mind was now made up
about the case, although what his conclusions were was more than
I could even dimly imagine. Several times during our homeward
journey I endeavoured to sound him upon the point, but he always
glided away to some other topic, until at last I gave it over in
despair. It was not yet three when we found ourselves in our
rooms once more. He hurried to his chamber and was down again in
a few minutes dressed as a common loafer. With his collar turned
up, his shiny, seedy coat, his red cravat, and his worn boots, he
was a perfect sample of the class.

"Capital!" said he. "I have the first link of my chain, and I am off to secure the second. I have been out to Streatham again since I saw you last, but I did not call at the house. It is a very sweet little problem, and I would not have missed it for a good deal. However, I must not sit gossiping here, for I must abjure these outward symbols of amateur mendicancy and return to my more respectable self." He vanished up the stairs, and a few minutes later I heard the hall door shut behind him.

"Great," said he. "I have been to the West End and have seen the person whom I particularly wished to see. I have also been to the City and have done a little business there. Everything is going as well as possible, and I think that the end of our journey is in sight. I shall be back late, Watson, for I have still a good deal to do." He swallowed his tea, snatched up his hat, and was off again in an instant, leaving me to my own reflections and the silent company of the fire.

"Greatly, Watson, greatly. I have already secured the most important link in my chain. That boot which you see in the corner is a key to the whole mystery, and I have high hopes that before the night is out I shall be able to tell you the name of the man who left its fellow in the snow of the stable lane. But time is pressing, and I must be off again if I am to catch my man before he has time to dispose of the property." And with a wave of his hand he was out of the room and down the stairs before I could ask him another question.

"Capital! I have the threads in my hand. I am only now beginning to see that there is a possibility of a happy ending. I have been to Streatham, and I have also been to the City. I have still much to do, but I hope to have everything clear by the morning. Good-bye for the present." He snatched up his hat and was gone before I could ask him another question.

"Oh, so-so. It is a matter of time and patience. I have the thread in my hands, and it will be strange if I do not find the end of it. I shall see you in the morning, Watson." He caught up his stick and was gone. I sat for some time by the fire, musing over the strange chain of events, but my friend's movements were always so rapid and his motives so complex that I felt it was useless to attempt to follow them. It was long after midnight when I heard the latch-key turn in the lock, and he stole quietly to his room.

"Oh, so so. Nothing to complain of. I have been out to Streatham
since I saw you last, but I did not call at the house. It is a
very sweet little problem, and I would not have missed it for a
good deal. However, I must not sit gossiping here, but must get
these disreputable clothes off and return to my highly
respectable self."

I had retired to my bed when I heard the latch-key in the lock
and his light footsteps on the stairs. He seemed to have had a
long journey and a hard one, but I did not ask him what his
fortune had been. In the morning he was up early and went out
once more before I had finished my breakfast.

"Well, Watson," said he as he re-entered the room about nine
o'clock, "the banker is just coming. Do you not hear his step? I
hope that we shall have good news for him."

The footsteps which I heard upon the stairs were slow and
measured. A moment later the door was opened, and Mr. Holder
entered the room.

"Well, Mr. Holmes," said he. "I have come to hear your verdict."

"You would prefer to wait a little, would you not?" said Holmes.

"No, I cannot wait any longer. Tell me everything."

"Then, first, let us see if we have not something for you."

"What! You have found the jewels?"

"I think so."

"You have found them! Oh, how can I thank you! You have saved
not only me but my client."

"You will find them in that corner," said Holmes, pointing to
where he had thrown the old boot.

"The jewels!" The banker was beside himself with joy. "But they
are not there!"

"No, but they are in this little case." Holmes took a small
morocco case from his pocket and laid it upon the table. The
banker opened it, and three magnificent beryls fell out into the
palm of his hand.

"Oh, thank God! thank God!" he cried, and fell into a chair. "I
could never have believed it possible. How did you find them?
Where did they come from?"

"That I will tell you presently," said Holmes. "First of all, I
think that we have something more to do. Is it not so, Watson?"

"I am as much in the dark as Mr. Holder is."

"Wait a little, and you will both be enlightened. Now, Mr.
Holder, will you please look at this letter? It was given to me
last night by your niece."

"By Mary? Is she in this also?"

"You had better read it for yourself."

The banker took the letter and read it. It was a short note
addressed to Sir George Burnwell, and was in Mary's handwriting.
In it she spoke of her love for him and of her desire to fly
with him, and she ended by saying that she had given him what he
asked for.

"Oh, the traitress!" cried the banker. "The wretched girl! She
has deceived me as well as my son. But where is Arthur? Why is
he silent if he is innocent?"

"That also I will explain to you," said Holmes. "But first let
us see what Arthur has to say for himself."

"But he is in prison!"

"No, I think not. I believe that he is in the next room. Come
in, Arthur."

The door opened and the banker's son entered the room. He was
very pale and looked as if he had undergone a terrible ordeal,
but there was a look of pride and resolution in his face which
showed that he was no longer the wild, wayward boy he had once
been.

"Oh, Arthur!" cried his father, "can you ever forgive me?"

"I have nothing to forgive, dad. I was as much to blame as
anyone."

"But why did you not speak? Why did you not tell me the truth?"

"Because I had promised Mary that I would never reveal her
secret. I could not break my word even to save myself from
prison."

"My boy! My brave, noble boy!" The banker threw his arms round
his son's neck and wept for joy.

"And now, Mr. Holmes," said he, "tell us how you found the
jewels and how you discovered the truth."

"It was a very simple matter," said Holmes, "although it
appeared to be so complex. When I first heard your story I was
convinced that your son was innocent. No man would have been so
foolish as to return to the room where he had committed a
robbery and to expose himself to the danger of being caught.
Besides, as I showed you, it would have been impossible for him
to have broken the coronet without making a noise which would
have awakened you.

"I then turned my attention to the others who were in the house.
Your niece, Mary, seemed to me to be the most likely person. She
had a motive, for she was in love with Sir George Burnwell, and
she had the opportunity, for she knew where the coronet was kept.
I also discovered that she had been in the habit of meeting Sir
George in the stable lane at night.

"When I went to Streatham I examined the stable lane and found
the tracks of a man and a woman in the snow. I also found the
track of a man with a wooden leg, which confirmed my suspicion
that the green-grocer's sweetheart was also involved.

"I then went to Sir George Burnwell's house and, by a little
strategy, I managed to get into his room. I found the beryls in
a drawer of his dressing-table. He had evidently intended to
sell them and to fly with Mary.

"As for Mary, she had already left your house and joined Sir
George. I have no doubt that they are now far away from England.

"And now, Mr. Holder, I think that our task is finished. Your
son is free, and your jewels are restored to you. I hope that in
the future you will be more careful in the choice of your
investments."

"I shall never forget what you have done for me, Mr. Holmes,"
said the banker. "You have saved my honour and my son's life."

"It was a very interesting case," said Holmes, "and I am glad
that I was able to be of service to you. And now, Watson, I
think that we have had enough of the Beryl Coronet. Let us turn
our attention to something more profitable."

I waited until midnight, but there was no sign of my friend. It was not until the early hours of the morning that I heard the click of his latch-key and his step upon the stair. When I descended to breakfast, I found him already at the table, preoccupied and silent. He had just finished his coffee when the door opened and Mr. Alexander Holder was shown in. If he had looked a pitiable object on the previous day, he was now a thousand times more so. His face was of a deathly pallor, his eyes were wild, and his hair was even more dishevelled than when he had first rushed into our presence.

I waited for him until past midnight, but he did not return. It was long after I had sought my own couch that I heard the remote clang of the street door and his quiet step as he ascended the stairs. In the morning, when I descended to our sitting-room, I found him already at the table, looking refreshed and triumphant, with a copy of the *Times* spread out before him and his coffee-cup steaming at his elbow. He looked up with a gleam in his eyes as I entered.

I waited for some time the next morning, but it was not until the clock was close upon the hour of nine that I heard the step of our client upon the stairs. He entered the room with a face so drawn and haggard that it was painful to look upon him. His eyes were bloodshot from a sleepless night, and his hands shook as he took the seat which I indicated. It was evident that the burden of his anxiety was becoming more than he could bear, and I was about to offer some word of sympathy when the door once more opened to admit Sherlock Holmes.

I waited for him until midnight, but there was no sign of his return. It was no unusual thing for him to be away for the whole night when he was on a hot scent, so I retired to my room. In the morning, however, I found him already in the sitting-room, looking somewhat pale and weary, but with a light of satisfaction in his eyes that told me his quest had not been in vain. He was busy at the side-table, but he turned with a smile as I entered.

I waited until midnight, but there was no sign of his return, so
I retired to my room. It was no uncommon thing for him to be away
for days and nights on end when he was hot upon a scent, so that
his lateness caused me no surprise. I do not know at what hour he
came in, but when I came down to breakfast in the morning there
he was with a cup of coffee in one hand and the paper in the
other, as fresh and trim as possible.

"You will excuse my beginning without you, Watson," said he, "but
you remember that our client has rather an early appointment this
morning."

"Why, it is after nine now," I answered. "I should not be
surprised if that were he. I thought I heard a ring."

"I do not know what I am to do," he groaned. "The suspense is more than I can bear. My son is in a cell, and the crown of England's treasure is defaced and incomplete. If the morning of Monday finds me without those gems, I am a lost man. My reputation, my position, my very life—all are at stake!" Holmes looked at him with a curious expression. "Have you the check-book there?" he asked. "I have it here." "Then I should be glad if you would draw me a check for four thousand pounds. It is a large sum, but the case has been an expensive one, and there are certain outlays which must be met."

"I am a broken man, Mr. Holmes," he groaned. "I care little for the money now, but the shame and the loss of my household are more than I can bear. Mary has gone—my dear Mary. She left me this morning, leaving only a short note to say that she could no longer endure the horror of our situation. I am left alone in my old age, with my son in a prison cell and my niece a fugitive."

"I do not know what I am to do!" he groaned. "The shame of it is more than I can bear. My son a thief, my niece's heart broken, and the gems still gone. I have been to the police, but they can tell me nothing. They only shake their heads and say that they have done all that can be done. It is the end of my honour and my life."

"I am a broken man, Mr. Holmes," he groaned, burying his face in his large, trembling hands. "The police have found no trace of the missing stones, and my son—my only son—remains as cold and silent as the grave. Mary is nearly distracted with grief, and the weight of this dishonour is more than I can bear. In a few short hours, I must face my illustrious client, and what can I tell him save that I have betrayed his confidence and ruined the greatest treasure of the empire?"

"I am a broken man, Mr. Holmes," he groaned, burying his face in his hands. "The blow has been too much for me. It is not enough that my son should be a thief and my reputation ruined, but now the very light of my life has been extinguished. Mary, my dear Mary, has left me. She is gone, Mr. Holmes, gone from my house, leaving only a few lines of despair to tell me that she could no longer bear the shame that has fallen upon our roof. My home is a desolation, and I am left alone in my old age to face the world's scorn."

"I do not know what I have done to be so severely tried," said
he. "Only two days ago I was a happy and prosperous man, without
a care in the world. Now I am left to a lonely and dishonoured
age. One sorrow comes close upon the heels of another. My niece,
Mary, has deserted me."

"Deserted you?"

"'My dearest uncle,' it ran, 'I feel that my presence here only adds to your sorrows. Since I cannot undo the past, and since my presence must always remind you of the dark cloud which has fallen upon our house, I have determined to leave you forever. Do not seek to follow me, for my resolution is fixed. Your unhappy Mary.' That was all she wrote, Mr. Holmes, and it has broken my heart. What can it mean? Is it possible that she, too, was in some way involved in this dreadful business?"

"'My dearest Uncle,—I feel that I have brought trouble upon you, and that if I had acted differently this terrible misfortune might never have occurred. I cannot, with this fatal conviction in my mind, continue to live under your roof, for I feel that I can no longer look you in the face. Your strange visitor of yesterday has, I believe, seen through the truth, and his presence has made my position even more intolerable. Do not seek to find me, for it will be useless. Kind as you have been to me, I feel that my path now lies elsewhere. Your ever affectionate, Mary.' What could she mean by it, Mr. Holmes? Do you think she means that she had taken her own life?"

"My dearest Uncle," it run, "I feel that I have brought trouble upon you, and that if I had acted differently this terrible misfortune might never have occurred. I cannot, with this wound in my mind, continue to live under your roof, and I feel I must leave you forever. Do not hope to trace me, for my throwing myself away will be a less grief to me than the thoughts of the misery I have brought upon you. With love, Mary." "What can she mean by that, Mr. Holmes? Do you think that she means she has taken her own life?"

"My Dearest Uncle,—I feel that I have brought trouble upon you, and that if I had acted differently this terrible misfortune might never have occurred. I cannot, with this wound in my mind, continue to live under your roof, and I can only hope that you will soon be able to forget your wretched Mary. What could she mean by it, Mr. Holmes? Do you think that she has committed suicide?"

"'My Dearest Uncle,—I feel that after what you said to me last night I can no longer remain under your roof. I know that I have been a cause of trouble to you, though God knows I never meant to be. Since you feel that Arthur’s ruin lies at my door, it is better that I should remove myself from your sight. Do not seek for me, for I am going to those who will cherish me. Your heartbroken Mary.'"

"'MY DEAREST UNCLE:--I feel that I have brought trouble upon you,
and that if I had acted differently this terrible misfortune
might never have occurred. I cannot, with this thought in my
mind, ever again be happy under your roof, and I feel that I must
leave you forever. Do not worry about my future, for that is
provided for; and, above all, do not search for me, for it will
be fruitless labour and an ill-service to me. In life or in
death, I am ever your loving,--MARY.'

"What could she mean by that note, Mr. Holmes? Do you think it
points to suicide?"

"No, no, nothing of the kind. It is perhaps the best possible
solution. I trust, Mr. Holder, that you are nearing the end of
your troubles."

"Ha! You say so! You have heard something, Mr. Holmes; you have
learned something! Where are the gems?"

"You would not think 1000 pounds apiece an excessive sum for
them?"

"I would pay ten."

"That would be unnecessary. Three thousand will cover the matter.
And there is a little reward, I fancy. Have you your check-book?
Here is a pen. Better make it out for 4000 pounds."

With a dazed face the banker made out the required check. Holmes
walked over to his desk, took out a little triangular piece of
gold with three gems in it, and threw it down upon the table.

With a shriek of joy our client clutched it up.

"You have it!" he gasped. "I am saved! I am saved!"

The reaction of joy was as passionate as his grief had been, and
he hugged his recovered gems to his bosom.

"There is one other thing you owe, Mr. Holder," said Sherlock
Holmes rather sternly.

"Owe!" He caught up a pen. "Name the sum, and I will pay it."

"He knows it already," said Holmes. "When I had cleared it all up I had an interview with him, and finding that he would not tell me the story, I told it to him, on which he admitted the correctness of it and added a few details which were not quite clear to me. Your morning's news, however, may certainly be a blow to him, for he has played the part of a hero throughout. But before you see him, it is only right that I should explain the mystery which has so nearly cost you your reputation and your son's freedom."

"He is already aware of the facts," Holmes remarked, checking the banker's impulsive movement. "I saw him at the station before coming here, and although he was initially unwilling to speak, he admitted everything once I showed him the recovered beryls. However, you must first understand the true nature of the events that took place under your roof, for your son's silence was a noble one, meant to protect you from an even deeper grief. It is time that the mask was stripped from the face of the man who is the real architect of your misfortune."

"Wait a bit," said Holmes. "There are one or two points which I should like to make clear to you before you go, for it is only right that you should know the true history of what has occurred under your roof. You have been very near to a great disaster, and it is only by a miracle that you have escaped it. As to your son, he is already aware that his innocence is known, for I have taken the liberty of sending a message to the inspector in charge of the case. Sit down, then, and I will tell you in a few words how the matter stands, and how I came to possess these gems which you see before you."

"One moment," said Holmes, laying his hand upon the banker's arm. "There are some points which must be cleared up before you leave this room. You have done your son a great injustice, but you were not the only one who was deceived. It was a very clever and a very heartless conspiracy, and had it not been for the snow, which is the detective's best friend, it might have remained a mystery to the end of time." He turned to me with a smile. "You remember, Watson, that I was particularly interested in the tracks in the stable lane?"

"Wait a bit," said Holmes. "We have still a little more to say. You owe it to your son, and you owe it to me, to understand how this matter really stands. You saw your son with the coronet in his hands, but you did not see what had happened a few minutes before. You did not see that the window was open, and that your niece, Mary, whom you have so cherished, had handed the treasure to her lover, Sir George Burnwell, through that very window."

"He knows it already. When I had cleared it all up I had an
interview with him, and finding that he would not tell me the
story, I told it to him, on which he had to confess that I was
right and to add the very few details which were not yet quite
clear to me. Your news of this morning, however, may open his
lips."

"For heaven's sake, tell me, then, what is this extraordinary
mystery!"

"It is the unfortunate truth," said Holmes, leaning back and joining his fingertips. "When I examined the snow in the stable lane, I found two distinct sets of tracks. One belonged to a man with a wooden leg—the green-grocer, no doubt, who had come to see the maid. But the other, far more significant, were the traces of a man in evening boots who had waited long by the hall window. Beside them were the light, dainty prints of a woman’s slippers. It was clear that an assignation had taken place, and when I saw the window sill was marred by the pressure of a man's weight, I knew that the coronet had not been taken from within by a thief, but handed out to a confederate."

"It is a hard truth to face," Holmes continued, his voice softened by a rare touch of sympathy. "But the evidence of the snow was beyond dispute. While you and Watson were indoors, I was reading a very plain story written upon the white surface of the lane. There were the tracks of a man who had waited long by the wall, and the lighter prints of a woman who had come to the hall window to meet him. More than that, I found where a heavy object had been dropped and then recovered. It became evident to me that your niece, under the spell of a man who is as heartless as he is handsome, had agreed to provide him with the means to settle his own desperate gambling debts. She had reached for the coronet not for herself, but for Sir George Burnwell."

"It is, unfortunately, more than a mere possibility; it is a certainty," Holmes replied, his voice grave. "When I arrived at Fairbank, my first care was to examine the snow, which, as a record of the night’s events, was as clear to me as a printed page. I found the footprints of two distinct men in the stable lane. One set was the heavy, uneven tread of the green-grocer with the wooden leg, but the other was the sharp, clear impression of a man’s evening boots. This second man had waited for a considerable time under the hall window, pacing back and forth as if in great agitation. Most significant of all, I found where a woman’s light foot had pressed near the sill and where she had leaned out to communicate with the man who stood waiting in the darkness."

"It is, unfortunately, the only possible conclusion," said Holmes. "When I walked round the house yesterday, I found clear evidence in the snow of the stable lane. There were two sets of tracks: one made by a man in evening boots, and the other by a lady in light shoes. The man had waited by the wall, while the lady had come to the hall window—the very window, you remember, which I examined so closely. I followed the man's tracks and found that they led straight to the house which Sir George Burnwell has been occupying. My visit to the West End last night was to confirm the pattern of his footwear, and I found, as I expected, that the soles of his boots corresponded exactly with the impressions I had seen in the slush."

I fear it is only too true," Holmes replied gravely. "The tracks in the snow told a story that could not be misread. There were the prints of a woman's light shoes and the heavier tread of a man's boot meeting repeatedly in the stable lane. I traced the man's steps to the very window where your niece stood on the night of the theft. It became clear to me that Sir George Burnwell had established a powerful hold over her. He is a man of desperate character beneath his polished exterior, and he saw in the Beryl Coronet a means to escape the financial ruin brought on by his own profligacy. It was he who persuaded her to take the gems from your bureau and pass them to him through the window.

"It is unfortunately more than possible; it is certain. Neither
you nor your son knew the true character of this man when you
admitted him into your family circle. He is one of the most
dangerous men in England--a ruined gambler, an absolutely
desperate villain, a man without heart or conscience. Your niece
knew nothing of such men. When he breathed his vows to her, as he
had done to a hundred before her, she flattered herself that she
alone had touched his heart. The devil knows best what he said,
but at least she became his tool and was in the habit of seeing
him nearly every evening."

"I cannot, and I will not, believe it!" cried the banker with an
ashen face.

She waited until the house was silent, then she stole into your dressing-room, unlocked the bureau, and carried the coronet down to the hall window. Sir George Burnwell was waiting in the lane, and to him she handed the precious treasure. But she was not unobserved. Your son, Arthur, had been unable to sleep and had seen his cousin's movements. He followed her down, saw the transfer, and, without a thought for his own safety or even his attire, he sprang out into the snow and pursued the baronet. There was a fierce struggle in the darkness, and Arthur succeeded in wrenching the coronet from the villain’s grasp, but not before a portion of the gold had been snapped off and remained in Sir George's hand.

When you had finally retired to your room, the girl, driven by her desperate passion, stole back to the bureau. She made use of the key which Arthur had so inadvertently suggested, and within moments the coronet was in her grasp. She hurried to the hall window and passed the treasure out to Sir George, who stood waiting in the lane. But she had been followed. Arthur, whose heart was heavy and who had remained awake, saw her flit past his door. Suspecting some ill-intent, he rushed after her and reached the window just as the exchange was completed.

After you had retired, she waited until the house was hushed before descending once more to the dressing-room. With the ease of one who knows the household intimately, she secured the treasure and carried it to the window, where Sir George was waiting. Your son, however, was not asleep; the double burden of his debts and his concern for Mary kept him restless. Hearing a movement, he observed his cousin's flight and followed her, only to witness the coronet being passed into the hands of a man in the darkness. Without pausing to dress, he sprang through the door and pursued the shadow down the lane, determined to retrieve the family's honour at any cost.

"Your son, however, had been unable to sleep, his mind being filled with his own troubles and his father's stern refusal. He heard a light step pass his door, and, looking out, he was amazed to see his cousin stealing down the passage with the morocco case in her hand. Stunned by the sight, he followed her in his stocking-feet and saw her from the shadow of the hall as she opened the window and passed the treasure to someone who waited outside. He rushed forward, but she had already closed the sash and fled past him in the darkness, seeking the refuge of her own chamber. Arthur, realizing that the family honour was at stake, did not hesitate for a second. He tore open the window, leaped out into the snow just as he was, and pursued the retreating figure which he saw through the gloom of the lane."

"When the house was still, she crept to your room, opened the bureau, and took the coronet. She carried it down to the window where Sir George was waiting. Arthur, however, had not gone to sleep. From his room he heard the soft footfall and, suspicious of his cousin's late-night movements, followed her. He arrived just as she was handing the coronet through the open window to her lover. With a cry of horror, he sprang forward and grappled with the man outside. In the fierce struggle that followed, as each man hauled at the golden circlet, it snapped, leaving a small fragment in Arthur’s hand while Sir George fled into the night with the rest."

"Your boy, Arthur, went to bed after his interview with you but
he slept badly on account of his uneasiness about his club debts.
In the middle of the night he heard a soft tread pass his door,
so he rose and, looking out, was surprised to see his cousin
walking very stealthily along the passage until she disappeared
into your dressing-room. Petrified with astonishment, the lad
slipped on some clothes and waited there in the dark to see what
would come of this strange affair. Presently she emerged from the
room again, and in the light of the passage-lamp your son saw
that she carried the precious coronet in her hands. She passed
down the stairs, and he, thrilling with horror, ran along and
slipped behind the curtain near your door, whence he could see
what passed in the hall beneath. He saw her stealthily open the
window, hand out the coronet to someone in the gloom, and then
closing it once more hurry back to her room, passing quite close
to where he stood hid behind the curtain.

"It is the only theory which covers the facts," Holmes replied, leaning back and joining his fingertips. "Your son's silence, his refusal to defend himself, and even his request for those five minutes of grace—which were intended for a desperate search in the snow for the missing gems—all become intelligible. He had managed to wrest the coronet from the thief, but in the struggle, the corner had snapped off. He returned to his room, intending to see if the damage could be repaired, only to be confronted by your own sudden appearance and accusations."

"It is more than possible; it is the truth," said Holmes. "Your son, in his chivalrous devotion to his cousin, preferred to face the charge of theft rather than to blacken her name by telling the truth. He knew that she was under the spell of this villain, and he hoped, no doubt, that if he could but recover the gems, the whole matter might be hushed up without her being implicated. He did not realize that by his silence he was leaving you in an agony of suspense and himself in the shadow of the dock. As for me, my task was to trace the missing stones, and for that purpose, I visited Sir George Burnwell in the guise which you saw me assume yesterday."

"It is more than possible; it is the only explanation which covers all the facts," Holmes answered. "When I saw the tracks in the snow, the whole thing became clear to me. There were the marks of a man in boots, who had stood for some time under the window, and there were the tracks of a man in bare feet, who had pursued him. I could see where they had struggled, and where the snow had been all trampled and tossed. The bare feet were your son's, and the boots were Sir George's. He had waited there for the coronet to be handed out to him, and he had been surprised by Arthur while he was still holding it."

"It is more than possible; it is the truth," said Holmes. "Your son's motive for silence was the most noble of all. He knew that to clear himself he must ruin the woman he loved—your niece. He chose rather to face the shame and the prison than to speak the word which would have broken her heart and yours. It was only when I showed him that I knew all, and that the gems were recovered, that he could be brought to see that his silence was no longer a duty."

"It is more than possible; it is certain," Holmes replied. "I was fortunate enough to be able to find a very distinct trail in the snow. You remember that I spent some time in the stable lane? There were the footmarks of a man with a wooden leg, which were obviously those of the green-grocer, but there were also the tracks of a man in boots, and of another in his bare feet. The man in boots had stood for some time under the window, where the snow was all trampled. The man in his bare feet had run out from the window, and there were the marks of a struggle between the two. The man in boots had then run off down the lane, while the man in his bare feet had returned to the house. It was all as clear as possible."

"You then roused his anger by calling him names at a moment when
he felt that he had deserved your warmest thanks. He could not
explain the true state of affairs without betraying one who
certainly deserved little enough consideration at his hands. He
took the more chivalrous view, however, and preserved her
secret."

"I found," said Holmes, "that the snow offered a most instructive record of the night's events. There were the tracks of a man in evening boots who had waited long by the window, and those of your niece who had joined him. Then came the frantic, light impressions of a barefooted man—your son—and the unmistakable signs of a violent struggle during which the coronet was wrenched asunder. I followed the tracks of the man in boots to the road, where I obtained a perfect impression of a very characteristic heel-plate. With this clue, I returned to London, adopted the disguise of a common loafer, and sought out the stables of Sir George Burnwell. There I managed to secure one of his boots, which matched the print exactly, and learned from his groom that his master had returned late with a significant injury to his head."

"When I arrived at Fairbank," said Holmes, "the snow was a perfect register of all that had occurred. I saw the tracks of the wooden leg of Francis Prosper, but they were confined to the area near the kitchen and had no bearing on the theft. Far more significant were the traces in the stable lane, where I saw the prints of a man's boots and, beside them, the distinct marks of your son's bare feet. There was every sign of a fierce struggle, and I followed the boot-marks until they led me directly to the residence of Sir George Burnwell. I was already convinced of his guilt, but I had yet to recover the missing beryls. My second visit to Streatham, in the disguise of a common loafer, enabled me to observe the household and confirm that Sir George had indeed been wounded in the face, just as your son had described."

"I followed the tracks," continued Holmes, "and they led me to a certain house not far from your own. I had already formed my own conclusions as to the identity of the man in the boots, for your son's description of his friend's character, combined with the fact that he was the only frequent visitor, pointed directly to Sir George Burnwell. I visited him in the guise which you saw me assume yesterday, and I was fortunate enough to find him at home. He had a strip of court-plaster over his eye, which was a very suggestive piece of evidence. I taxed him with the robbery, and after some little pressure, I was able to convince him that the game was up."

"As you observed, my first action at the scene was to examine the lane," Holmes explained. "The fresh snow acted as a silent witness to the night's events. I identified the lingering footprints of a man who had waited for some time near the window, joined later by the frantic tracks of another. The evidence of a violent encounter was unmistakable; the ground was churned up, and I even discovered traces of blood. It was evident that the man in boots had fled toward the road in great haste, whereas the bare footprints—which I knew to be Arthur's—led directly back to the house. This confirmed that your son was the hero of the piece, having chased down the intruder to reclaim the treasure."

"When I arrived at your house," Holmes continued, "I at once examined the snow in the stable lane. It was a perfect register of all that had occurred. I saw where a lady had stood at the window, and I saw the tracks of the man who had waited for her. I could see that he had been there for some time. Then I saw the traces of the struggle, and the footprints of the man who had run away. Most importantly, I observed that while one of the combatants was barefoot, the other wore boots, one of which had a very characteristic cast. It was by following these tracks and identifying that specific boot-mark that I was able to trace the second man to his residence."

"When I arrived at the house," continued Holmes, "I at once went
very carefully round it to observe if there were any traces in
the snow which might help me. I knew that none had fallen since
the evening before, and also that there had been a strong frost
to preserve impressions. I passed along the tradesmen's path, but
found it all trampled down and indistinguishable. Just beyond it,
however, at the far side of the kitchen door, a woman had stood
and talked with a man, whose round impressions on one side showed
that he had a wooden leg. I could even tell that they had been
disturbed, for the woman had run back swiftly to the door, as was
shown by the deep toe and light heel marks, while Wooden-leg had
waited a little, and then had gone away. I thought at the time
that this might be the maid and her sweetheart, of whom you had
already spoken to me, and inquiry showed it was so. I passed
round the garden without seeing anything more than random tracks,
which I took to be the police; but when I got into the stable
lane a very long and complex story was written in the snow in
front of me.

On entering the house, I examined, as you remember, the sill and framework of the hall window with my lens. I could at once see that someone had passed out, but it was the sill itself which gave me the most valuable clue. There were several small scratches upon the wood, such as might be made by the hard pressure of a gem. This confirmed my view that the coronet had been passed through the window.
