I then visited the stables of Sir George Burnwell and, in my character of a loafer, I managed to secure that old boot which you saw me bring back. I found that it fitted the marks in the lane to a nicety, and my case was complete.

"On entering the house I examined, as you remember, the shoes of
the household, but none of them at all corresponded to those
marks. I had, however, seen Sir George Burnwell's boots in the
hall when I was here yesterday, and I was convinced that it was
his track which I had followed. I then asked to see your son's
feet, and though they were somewhat swollen from the cold, there
could be no doubt that he was the man who had run out into the
snow. Everything was now clear. Sir George Burnwell had obtained
the coronet from Miss Mary, he had been followed by Arthur, and
in the struggle which ensued a corner of the gold had been
broken off and had remained in the boy's hand. He had rushed
back and tried to straighten the diadem, but his father had
entered and had at once accused him of the theft."

On entering the house, I examined, as you remember, the sill and framework of the hall window with my lens, and I could at once see that someone had passed out. I could distinguish the outline of an instep where the wet foot had been placed upon the wood. I was then certain that my theory was correct. The next thing was to identify the wearer of the boots. From your description of Sir George Burnwell, I had already suspected him, and my visit to his house in the guise of a loafer confirmed my fears. I saw his groom cleaning a pair of boots in the yard, and a single glance was enough to show me that they were the same which had left their traces in the snow. I then obtained an interview with Sir George himself. He was a man of iron nerve, and at first he laughed my accusations to scorn; but when I showed him that I was acquainted with every particular of his conduct, and that I had the means of proving it, his manner changed. He confessed that in the struggle with your son the corner of the coronet had snapped off in his hand, and that he had fled with the three gems, leaving the rest in Arthur's grasp.

"I then visited the house of Sir George Burnwell, where I found that my suspicions were fully confirmed. He had a fresh wound upon his forehead, and his boots were the exact counterparts of those which I had measured in the snow. I followed him to a certain dealer's in the City, and, as soon as he had left the shop, I entered it myself. I found that he had just disposed of three beryls for a small sum. I had some difficulty in persuading the dealer to part with them, but at last, by the payment of three thousand pounds, I was able to secure them and bring them away with me."

"But how did you find out who the man was?" asked the banker.
"I will tell you. When I returned to town, I at once changed my
dress and went out to see Sir George Burnwell. I had already
identified his footmark in the snow, for I had had an
opportunity of seeing his boots during a previous visit to your
house. I knew that it was he, and no other. He was, as I had
expected, in a state of considerable nervous tension. I told him
at once that I knew all, and that his only chance of escaping
the police was to give up the gems. He blustered at first, but
when I showed him that I possessed the boot which he had worn
that night—for I had successfully bribed his valet to let me
have it—and when I pointed out the bloodstain upon his cuff, he
saw that the game was up. He confessed that he had already parted
with the stones, but he gave me the address of the man who had
bought them."

"On entering the house, however, I examined, as you remember, the
sill and framework of the hall window with my lens, and I could
at once see that someone had passed out. I could distinguish the
outline of an instep where the wet foot had been placed in coming
in. I was then beginning to be able to form an opinion as to what
had occurred. A man had waited outside the window; someone had
brought the gems; the deed had been overseen by your son; he had
pursued the thief; had struggled with him; they had each tugged
at the coronet, their united strength causing injuries which
neither alone could have effected. He had returned with the
prize, but had left a fragment in the grasp of his opponent. So
far I was clear. The question now was, who was the man and who
was it brought him the coronet?

"I then dressed myself in my old clothes and went down to
Streatham as a man with a wooden leg. There I found the
green-grocer, and learned from him that the maid, Lucy Parr, was
entirely innocent. In the course of our talk he mentioned to me
that Sir George Burnwell had been several times lately. This
confirmed my suspicions, so I at once set to work to see how I
could bring him to book. I knew that he was a man who would set
his wits against mine, and I should have to be very careful. He
is a man who has lived at the rate of several thousands a year,
and yet has no known source of income. It was clear that he had
been living on his wits for some time and that he was an
accomplished scoundrel. I followed him up and soon found that
the gems had been disposed of. He had already found a customer
for them, and it was only by my offering him more than the price
which he had agreed to take that I could induce him to part with
them. The third gem he had already given to a friend of his, but
he was able to get it back for me by my giving him the same sum.
I then returned to my rooms with the gems, and after our talk of
this morning I went to see your son and told him all that I had
learned."

"The man, then, must have been her lover. He was a person whom
Arthur knew, as was proved by his silence; but more than that, he
was a person who was likely to be a man of fashion and to be
well-known. Such a man would not be a mere common thief. His
vices, as you have described them, point to a man of the world.
And when I recalled your mention of Sir George Burnwell, I began
to have some hope that I might be upon the right scent. He was a
man whom your son hated and your niece admired, and who, with his
debts and his position, would be just the man to be tempted by
such a treasure. There was but one thing more to be proved, and
that was that he was the person whose track I had followed. I
visited him that morning, as you know, in my disguise of a
common fellow, but I did not go to his house. I went to the end
of the lane and there, by good fortune, I was just in time to see
the green-grocer's boy who has the round impression of a wooden
leg, as I told you. He had a conversation with a girl, and I
followed her to the house and saw her enter. It was Lucy Parr,
your waiting-maid. I was satisfied then that I was upon the
right track. My next business was to identify the boots. I
managed to see the foot-marks of Sir George's groom, and I
recognised the same size and shape as those I had seen in the
snow. So I was satisfied on that score."

"The next point was, who was her lover? And who could it be but
the one man of her acquaintance who was a man of the world, a man
of bad reputation, a gambler, and a spendthrift? That Sir George
Burnwell was the man I was now certain. I felt that if I could
once get to him the rest would be easy. My next step was to see
the green-grocer with the wooden leg, because I thought that he
might have seen some third person hanging about the house, and
so it was. I found that he had seen a tall, dark man who was
talking to a woman in the lane, but he could tell me nothing
more. It then occurred to me that I might be able to find
something out about this Sir George Burnwell by a little careful
observation. I visited his house as a common loafer, and there I
found that he had been hurt recently and that he had been for
some time in a state of high nervous tension. This, with the fact
that he was known to have large debts, was almost conclusive
evidence against him. I then proceeded to make certain inquiries
at various low-class pawnbrokers', but for a long time without
result. At last, however, I came across a man in the Ratcliffe
Highway who had a triangular piece of gold with three beryls in
it. I managed to get it from him for a price, and I then hurried
to the house of Sir George Burnwell and informed him that I knew
everything. He was at first defiant, but when I produced the
triangular piece of gold and told him that his name was in my
hands, he was glad to be allowed to go upon the payment of the
money which he had received for it. I then had an interview with
your son, and I found that I was right in all my conclusions.
I also found that he would not say anything for fear of
implicating his cousin, but that he was grateful for what I had
done for him. He will be released to-day."

"I then set off for Streatham as a common loafer, and soon found
the man I wanted. I went into his stables and found the boots
which corresponded with the impressions I had seen. They were a
peculiar pair with a large iron heel, such as no one but a person
of rank and wealth would wear. From the stables I followed the
clue to the house. I had no difficulty in learning that Sir
George Burnwell was on terms of great intimacy with the family. I
found that he had a slight wound over his right eye, which confirmed
my suspicions. I then saw your son, who at first would tell me
nothing, but at last confessed the whole story. He had seen his
cousin hand the coronet to Sir George through the window. He had
followed him, and they had a desperate struggle in the lane. Sir
George had escaped, but not before your son had managed to wrench
the coronet from his grasp, though in the struggle it had
snapped. Sir George had fled with the missing piece, and your son
had returned with the remainder. But he would not speak, for he
loved his cousin and would not bring disgrace upon her name. Now,
however, that she has fled with her lover, there is no longer any
reason for silence."

"But then who was the man who had waited for her, and who was it
he had struggled with? It must have been some man who was an
intimate of yours, and yet not of your son's, for he had no
reason to spare any friend of his. I thought of your son's
club, where his companion, Sir George Burnwell, was known as a
man of many debts. I decided that this was the most likely
clue, so I went off to Streatham once more, but this time to find
Sir George himself. I found that he lived at a small house
nearly opposite yours, and that he was in the habit of walking
over to your garden-gate every evening. I found that he was also
in the habit of going into the city every morning and that he
drove a very neat tandem. I followed him up and soon had my hand
on the clue. He had gone into the city to see a well-known
money-lender, and as he was known as a regular visitor there I
at once guessed that he had been to see him for some special
purpose. I waited until he had left the office and then I went
in and had a short talk with the money-lender. He told me that
Sir George had brought him three beryls and that he had been
very anxious to have them back, but that he could not afford to
pay the price which the money-lender had asked for them. I found
that they were at that moment in the possession of the
money-lender, and as I knew that you were prepared to pay 3000
pounds to recover them, I had no difficulty in getting them. I
gave him my check for the amount and brought the gems back to
Baker Street."

"And who could it be who was her confederate? A lover evidently,
for who else could outweigh the love and gratitude which she must
feel to you? I knew that you went out little, and that your
circle of friends was a very limited one. But among them was Sir
George Burnwell. I had heard of him before as being a man of evil
reputation among women. It must have been he who wore those boots
and retained the missing gems. Even though he knew that Arthur
had discovered him, he might still flatter himself that he was
safe, for the lad could not say a word without compromising his
own family.

"I returned to my rooms, resumed my own character, and drove at
once to the house of Sir George Burnwell," said Holmes. "I found
the baronet in his study, and the dark patch of sticking-plaster
above his brow told me that I had made no mistake in my man. At
first he was inclined to be insolent, but when I laid the facts
plainly before him and showed him that I had matched his tracks
and knew of his flight with your niece, he broke down completely.
He admitted that he had already disposed of the missing beryls to
a certain receiver in the City, a man whose name was already
familiar to me in connection with several shady transactions.
I forced him to give me the address, and then I left him to
make what preparations he could for the flight which I knew he
meditated."

"That was I," said Holmes. "I had an interview with Sir George Burnwell this morning. He was very high and mighty at first, but when I told him that I had evidence which would send him to penal servitude, he changed his tone. He admitted that he had the gems, but said that he had already sold them to a fence in the City. I got the address from him, and after some trouble and the payment of the sum I have mentioned, I managed to get them back. I then saw your son, and having told him that all was right, I came here to meet you."

"Exactly," said Holmes. "I then proceeded to the residence of Sir George Burnwell. I found him with a strip of sticking-plaster over his brow, which confirmed my deductions from the bloodstains in the snow. I did not mince words, but informed him that I was aware of his theft and that I was prepared to buy the missing fragment from him to avoid a public scandal. He attempted to bluster at first, but when I produced the pair of boots I had acquired and mentioned the struggle with your son, his defiance crumbled. He was a desperate man, and the prospect of three thousand pounds in cash proved more alluring than the risk of a police investigation. He handed over the gold piece with the beryls, and I left him to make his arrangements for the flight which, as we have seen, he has since carried out with your niece."

"I called upon Sir George Burnwell," Holmes continued, his voice dropping a note. "I found him with a very significant plaster over his brow. I did not mince words with him. I informed him that I held the evidence of his presence in the lane and that his only hope of avoiding a public trial lay in the restoration of the beryls. He was a desperate man, but he saw that the game was up. He attempted to argue, to deny, even to threaten, but in the end, the sight of my heavy hunting-crop and the promise of the police brought him to reason. He surrendered the three gems, and I allowed him to depart, knowing that his presence in London would soon be a thing of the past."

"I then returned to London, and having changed my clothes, I went to call upon Sir George Burnwell at his rooms. I found him in a very evil temper, with a bandage across his forehead where your son's blow had fallen. He attempted to bluster, but when I showed him that I held all the threads in my hand, and that I was prepared to use them, he soon changed his tone. He confessed that he had the stones, but that he had already sold them to a certain dealer in the City. I was able, however, by the use of your money and a little quiet persuasion, to discover where they were, and to redeem them from the hands of the receiver. I then returned to Baker Street, where I spent the rest of the night in your service."

"Precisely. It was I. I found that I had my man, so I came home
and changed my clothes. It was a delicate part which I had to
play then, for I saw that a prosecution must be avoided to avert
scandal, and I knew that so astute a villain would see that our
hands were tied in the matter. I went and saw him. At first, of
course, he denied everything. But when I gave him every
particular that had occurred, he tried to bluster and took down a
life-preserver from the wall. I knew my man, however, and I
clapped a pistol to his head before he could strike. Then he
became a little more reasonable. I told him that we would give
him a price for the stones he held--1000 pounds apiece. That
brought out the first signs of grief that he had shown. 'Why,
dash it all!' said he, 'I've let them go at six hundred for the
three!' I soon managed to get the address of the receiver who had
them, on promising him that there would be no prosecution. Off I
set to him, and after much chaffering I got our stones at 1000
pounds apiece. Then I looked in upon your son, told him that all
was right, and eventually got to my bed about two o'clock, after
what I may call a really hard day's work."

"I think that it is very likely that you will soon hear where she is," said Holmes. "Wherever Sir George Burnwell is, there is she also. You may be sure that a man of his character will soon make her regret the step she has taken. For yourself, you have a son who has shown himself to be a man of high and noble spirit. And now, Watson, I think that we have done enough for one morning. If you will reach me my violin, we shall see if we can forget for an hour the dark passions and the even darker tragedies of our fellow-men."

"I think that it is very probable that she is wherever Sir George Burnwell is," Holmes answered. "It is certain that she will find that she has bartered her peace of mind for a very miserable fate. For yourself, you have the comfort of knowing that the gems are safe and that your son has emerged from this ordeal with a character more truly noble than it has ever been before. As for me, I have found the case a most interesting one, and I shall be happy to add the check for four thousand pounds to my little collection of professional mementos." With a bow he showed our client to the door, and a few moments later he was back in his armchair, deep in the chemical research which our visitor's arrival had interrupted.

"I think that we may fairly surmise," said Holmes, "that she is wherever Sir George Burnwell is. It is equally certain, too, that whatever her sins are, they will soon receive a more than sufficient punishment. As for the coronet, it is now back in your possession, and I trust that you will lose no time in returning it to its illustrious owner. And now, Watson, I think that a little music might be beneficial to our nerves, for this case has been a somewhat exhausting one." With a curt nod, the banker hurried from the room, leaving us to our breakfast and the quiet of Baker Street.

"I think that it is very probable," said Holmes, "that she is wherever Sir George Burnwell is. It is certain that she is no longer at Fairbank. Let us hope that the lesson which she has learned may not be too late to save her from a life of misery. As for Sir George, he has the gems no longer, but he has the woman, and I fear that she will find him a more cruel master than even the law would have been. And now, Watson, I think that we have earned our breakfast, and I am sure that a little music will be a very pleasant change after the somewhat harsh experiences of the last two days. If you will have the kindness to reach me down my violin, we shall forget for a moment the darker side of London life in the harmonies of the masters."

"I think that we may safely say," returned Holmes, "that she is wherever Sir George Burnwell is. It is equally certain, too, that whatever her sins are, they will soon receive a more than sufficient punishment. For the rest, Mr. Holder, my advice to you is to remember that if you have lost a niece you have found a son, and that the next time you have a secret of state to keep you will do well to provide yourself with a more reliable lock for your bureau."
